I've always wondered, why the coffee industry doesn't standardize on "Percent of roast time related to the bean cracking stages"? What I mean is it's impossible to tell the roast level from the labels of roasted coffee, but as personal roaster, I always try to match a single origin coffee been roasting to 1st crack temp or % of development starting with 1st crack. This is what I could consider a medium roast. Anything before 1st crack is light roast. Anything between 1st and 2nd crack is medium and anything after 2nd crack is dark roast.
I would think it would be really easy to standardize on the percent of total roast time before 1st crack, then percent of total roast time after 1st crack (also called development time or %). Then Percent of total time after 2nd crack. This would tell you exactly what the roast level was. And based on the coffee origin, it would tell you exactly what the flavor profile would be at that roast level.

So at standards light roast may be 80% - 95% to first crack. Or you could say 20% to 5% to 1st crack. That would tell you it has citrus and acid. Then 20% development into 1st crack is what most specialty roasters go for, and likewise you could determine dark roast as development % past 2nd crack to see how burnt it really is.

Does this make sense to anyone else? It just seems so logical for labeling standard roast levels to me.

I used to work for a smaller commercial roaster in Seattle back in the 70's, which led me into the food industry as a line cook, a tea man, an R&D tester, professor, and eventually as a historian. I've often wondered if the roasting side of the business has yet taken full advantage of the computer controlled technology that's developed in manufacturing over the last several decades.
The machine control in all aspects of manufacturing should certainly enable specialty roasting control to parameters within the bean! For example, a high temp flash roast to just beyond first crack (shortened to 90 seconds, say), followed by cold temp air blast cooling, and then finishing with a slow roast to maintain terroir character and finish off the internals of the bean while bringing the exterior to the desired maillard flavor characteristics and roast color. What flavor would THAT roasting profile produce?
All quantifiable and repeatable, allowing multi-roast characteristics to be explored BETWEEN the surface and the interior of the bean.
